How do I get the XYZ position of my robot's tool tip?

I get $10,000 worth of measurements from a $40 drawing tablet. Now I want the height of the pen too.

How do I get the precise x, y, and z coordinates of the tip of my robot's gripper?

I use an SO-101, a small robot arm, to build a smooth, precise controller: the program that turns a desired path into motor commands. I call it the drawing arm project, but drawing is only one showcase. The controller should also work in space, so I want to move beyond the XY plane. Right now the gripper holds a pen, and a Wacom drawing tablet measures the pen's tip, called the nib. The tablet is a flat sensor that reports where the pen touches it, giving me x and y along its surface. What I'm missing is z, the height above that plane.

The tablet is also the best deal in my setup. It cost about US$40 and reports the pen position to within ±0.25 mm, 133 times a second. OptiTrack, a motion-capture system, lists ±0.3 mm for its cameras, and four of them cost about US$10,000 before software. The two figures come from different kinds of specification, but they sit in the same ballpark. That makes the tablet a cheap, precise feedback signal for learning precise motions, as long as the pen touches it.

Why measure the tip in space?

Tracking the tip's path lets me see how a change to the controller affects the motion. On the tablet, that tells me how well the arm draws. But the arm should also carry a tool above the table, so I want to measure its motion in free space and see whether corrections learned while drawing still help there. Those measurements also give me data to build a model of how the arm moves.

The arm already tells me something about its own pose through its encoders, the sensors that read each joint angle. The catch is that the arm can bend between a joint and the tip, changing the path. So I want an outside reference that measures the result of the whole chain, including the tool holder.

Three ways to measure in space

A friend who works on robots described three routes for measuring beyond the tablet plane. One uses a camera to locate a ChArUco board, a checkerboard with coded markers. Another puts markers on the arm and tracks them with sweeping base stations or infrared motion-capture cameras. The third uses a laser tracker that follows a reflector.

A camera and a ChArUco board

The codes on a ChArUco board tell the camera which part of the pattern it's looking at. The corners give it geometric reference points, and the known square size gives their spacing. Once the camera is calibrated, relating image coordinates to rays in space, I can use that known geometry to estimate the board's position and orientation. OpenCV ChArUco guide

In the sketch, a board beside the tablet sets a reference frame, and a target attached to the tool moves with it. The relation between the target and the nib is fixed, so I can use the target's pose to find the nib position. Several calibrated views add a triangulation baseline and help keep the target visible as the arm moves. Higher image resolution puts more samples across the target, but the geometry matters too. A sideways movement shifts the pattern across the image, while a change in depth changes its apparent scale. That makes the depth estimate sensitive to target size, viewing angle, and lens calibration.

For a small arm, I can use the tablet as a direct reference while drawing and a calibrated camera to measure above the surface. A phone such as the Pixel makes this possible without a dedicated motion-capture installation.

Markers and base stations or motion-capture cameras

The second route follows markers on the arm. Sweeping base stations send infrared laser scans across photodiodes on a tracker, and the system combines these observations with inertial measurements to estimate the tracker's position and orientation. SteamVR study

Infrared motion capture works differently. Cameras observe reflective markers and triangulate their positions, and a rigid cluster of non-collinear markers also gives the tool's orientation. OptiTrack marker tracking

A tracker can look stable while stationary and still have substantially larger errors when it moves. In the SteamVR study, the four-station setup reached 0.574 mm aggregate RMSE at 12.5 mm/s, rising to 4.237 mm at 50 mm/s. RMSE stands for root mean square error and gives large misses more weight than small ones. Since I want to track a moving tool, the dynamic result matters.

Where I put the markers determines which part of the mechanical chain the measurement includes. Markers near the tool measure its motion, while markers on separate arm links can also reveal where bending occurs.

A laser tracker

A laser tracker combines a distance measurement with angular encoders to locate the center of a reflector in space. A dedicated pose target adds orientation, which matters when the reflector is offset from a rotating tool tip. Hexagon tracker specifications

This is industrial dimensional measurement equipment, providing an independent metric reference with tight specified error bounds. The target and its mounting geometry are part of the measurement system too.

Comparing the systems

The figures describe different properties, so comparing the systems takes some care. Rate counts samples per second, while latency measures the time from a physical motion to a usable sample in the program. Mean absolute error (MAE) averages the size of the errors, and RMSE gives large misses more weight. A tolerance or maximum permissible error states a bound under specified conditions. The two charts show the spread, and the table below them keeps each figure with its source link.

What the US$40 buys

Inside its plane, the tablet quotes accuracy in the same ballpark as a motion-capture system that costs more than 200 times as much.

  • Accuracy: the tablet lists ±0.25 mm and OptiTrack PrimeX 13 lists ±0.3 mm. The tablet's figure is a tolerance bound and OptiTrack's is a typical value, so they are comparable quoted specifications, not a measured tie.
  • Price: the tablet cost me about US$40. Four PrimeX 13 cameras cost US$9,996 at list price, plus US$1,148 for the Motive:Tracker software and key.
  • Resolution: Wacom lists 100 lines per mm, which is 0.01 mm. That is much finer than its accuracy, so the pen reports small moves that the sensor does not claim to place exactly.

The tablet does not win everywhere. OptiTrack tracks in three dimensions and samples at 240 Hz, compared with the tablet's 133. The Leica laser tracker has a specified error bound of 0.021 mm at 1 m, more than ten times tighter than the tablet's, and costs US$17k to 75k.

From the sensor target to the nib

These systems track a target near the nib, so I still need the geometric relation between what the sensor sees and the point I care about. If the target position is ttt, its rotation is RRR, and the nib offset in target coordinates is rrr, then

pnib=t+Rr.p_{\text{nib}} = t + Rr. pnib​=t+Rr.

An error in the estimated orientation rotates that offset and shifts the estimated nib position, so keeping the target close to the nib reduces this lever arm. Timing matters too: a delayed sample describes where the tool was, so speed turns the delay into apparent path error.

Limits

  • Camera depth is the weakest point of the accessible route. Image resolution alone does not establish depth accuracy, and lens calibration, rolling shutter, occlusion, target orientation, and holder flex all affect the result. The ChArUco paper measured a different calibration rig than a Pixel tracking this arm.
  • The reference point and the error metric matter. The tablet has its own tolerance and supplies no calibrated height or tilt. Camera and tracker figures apply to their targets, and a rigid offset cannot account for flex between target and nib. Accuracy, repeatability, and the table's error metrics describe different properties.
  • The quoted conditions differ. SteamVR results include coordinate and sample-rate post-processing. OptiTrack's product page and family sheet, which lists ±0.2 mm, differ. Leica's bound uses specified precision reflectors. None of these figures establishes nib accuracy on this arm.
  • Rate is not latency. OptiTrack's listed camera latency excludes the rest of the application, and the other cited sources do not establish end-to-end delay for the complete recording chains. Tracking volume also depends on visibility, and component prices exclude a complete installation.

Which route fits a small arm?

For a small arm like the SO-101, a calibrated camera offers an accessible way to measure beyond the drawing plane. A phone already provides the images, and coded targets give me a geometric reference. The tablet stays useful on the surface, where it measures the pen directly.

Sweeping base stations offer wider coverage with compact tracking hardware, though their dynamic error matters for precise paths. Optical motion capture provides synchronized views and rigid-body tracking, but requires a dedicated installation. A laser tracker fits work that needs an independent dimensional reference. The choice depends on the motion I want to measure, the point each system tracks, and the conditions behind its accuracy figures.
